title: THEY STOOD AT THE GATES OF HEAVEN… AND JESUS ACCUSED THEM OF LOCKING PEOPLE OUT.
paragraphs: THEY STOOD AT THE GATES OF HEAVEN… AND JESUS ACCUSED THEM OF LOCKING PEOPLE OUT.
The terrifying warning of Matthew 23:13, the danger of religion without redemption, and what happens when the people who claim to represent God become the very reason others walk away from Him.
Imagine spending your entire life searching for God, only to discover that the people you trusted to lead you toward Him were standing in your way.

Imagine carrying the unbearable weight of your past, gathering enough courage to enter a place of worship, hoping to find forgiveness, only to leave feeling more condemned, unwanted, and spiritually unworthy than when you arrived.
Imagine being hungry for grace but being served judgment. Thirsty for truth but being offered religious performance. Desperate for healing but being reminded of every wound you carry.
Now imagine Jesus witnessing all of it.
What would He say?
We don't have to imagine His answer.
He already gave it.

“But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.” — Matthew 23:13 (KJV)
These were not the words of an atheist attacking Christianity. They were not the accusations of someone who hated Scripture or rejected holiness.
These were the words of Jesus Christ Himself.
And perhaps the most disturbing part of this passage is that Jesus was not speaking to people who had never heard of God.
He was speaking to religious experts.
People who studied Scripture. People who prayed publicly. People who understood religious traditions. People whom others looked toward for spiritual direction.
They knew the language of holiness.
Yet they were resisting the Holy One standing before them.
They possessed knowledge about God while opposing the very One who came to reveal Him.
And Jesus was not silent.
The original Greek text of Matthew 23:13 begins with a deeply unsettling expression:
Οὐαὶ δὲ ὑμῖν, γραμματεῖς καὶ Φαρισαῖοι, ὑποκριταί.
Ouai de hymin, grammateis kai Pharisaioi, hypokritai.
“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites.”

The Greek word οὐαί (ouai) is more than an ordinary expression of disappointment. It is an exclamation of grief, denunciation, and impending judgment. In the biblical prophetic tradition, a declaration of woe exposes the seriousness of rebellion against God.
Jesus was not merely irritated by their behavior.
He was pronouncing a devastating spiritual warning.
Then comes the accusation:
κλείετε τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
Kleiete tēn basileian tōn ouranōn emprosthen tōn anthrōpōn.
“You shut the kingdom of heaven before people.”
The word κλείετε (kleiete) comes from κλείω (kleiō), meaning to shut or close.
The expression ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων means before people or in front of them.
The imagery is heartbreaking.
People are approaching, but the religious leaders are obstructing their entrance.

The kingdom of heaven in Matthew's Gospel is not merely a reference to a destination after death. It concerns God's reign, His sovereign authority, and the saving reality of His kingdom announced and revealed through Jesus Christ.

These leaders were not literally capable of overpowering God or controlling His eternal kingdom. Rather, through their teaching, hypocrisy, opposition to Jesus, and misuse of spiritual authority, they were obstructing people from recognizing and responding to God's saving truth.
They were supposed to help people understand God's Word.
Instead, they were becoming obstacles between people and the truth.
Luke records a closely related warning:
“Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.” — Luke 11:52
They had access to Scripture, but they were mishandling the very knowledge that should have directed people toward God.
And before we become comfortable condemning religious leaders from two thousand years ago, perhaps we should ask a question that might expose something uncomfortable within ourselves.
Have we ever made Jesus harder for someone else to see?
Have we ever used Scripture to win an argument rather than lovingly communicate the truth?
Have we ever treated someone's brokenness as an opportunity to demonstrate our own righteousness?
Have we ever demanded mercy for ourselves while refusing to extend it to someone else?
Have we ever been so determined to prove that we were right that we forgot what it meant to love?

This passage is not permission to despise Jewish people, condemn every Pharisee, or assume that all religious leaders are corrupt. Jesus was Jewish, His earliest disciples were Jewish, and His rebuke addressed particular patterns of hypocrisy and spiritual blindness.
Neither is it an attack against biblical obedience, sound doctrine, church leadership, or genuine holiness.
Jesus affirmed the importance of obedience while exposing the corruption of those who taught righteousness but refused to practice it faithfully.
In Matthew 23:4, He described leaders who placed heavy burdens on people's shoulders while refusing to help carry them.
In Matthew 23:5, He exposed religious works performed to gain public recognition.
In Matthew 23:23, He confronted those who meticulously observed tithing while neglecting the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
Notice that Jesus did not tell them to abandon obedience. He told them not to neglect what mattered while practicing the other things.
Their problem was not that they cared too much about God's holiness.
Their problem was that their religious performance had become disconnected from the heart of God's commands.
They had learned how to appear righteous without allowing God's truth to confront their pride.
And that danger did not disappear when the first century ended.
Somewhere today, a person is afraid to pray because someone convinced them that God could never forgive what they have done.
Somewhere, a young believer is silently battling temptation because they fear that admitting their struggle will make them unacceptable to everyone around them.
Somewhere, a woman carries the scars of spiritual abuse and cannot hear the word “church” without remembering what happened behind closed doors.
Somewhere, a man who has destroyed his marriage believes that repentance is pointless because everyone has already decided who he is.

Somewhere, someone is reading these words while remembering the moment they walked away from a religious community, not necessarily because they stopped searching for God, but because they could no longer endure the way people treated them in His name.
If that is part of your story, please understand something.
The failures of people who claimed to represent Jesus do not define the character of Jesus.
Their hypocrisy is not His holiness.
Their cruelty is not His compassion.
Their manipulation is not His authority.
Their refusal to forgive does not mean that Christ is unwilling to receive a repentant sinner.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37
The Greek expression translated “in no wise cast out” contains the emphatic construction οὐ μὴ (ou mē), expressing a strong negation.
Christ's promise is not a hesitant invitation.
He will certainly not cast out the one who comes to Him.
That does not mean Jesus approves of everything we have done. It does not mean repentance is unnecessary or that sin has suddenly become harmless.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness toward sinners, bringing forgiveness and teaching us to turn away from ungodliness and live transformed lives through Christ (Titus 2:11–14).
Jesus loves us too deeply to pretend that the sin destroying us is harmless.
But He also does not demand that we become spiritually flawless before coming to Him.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He calls the weary to Himself.
He calls the spiritually dead into life.
And He does what religious performance could never accomplish.
He saves.
Think about the scandalous scene in Luke 7:36–50.
Jesus was eating in the home of a Pharisee named Simon when a woman known in the city as a sinner approached Him.
She stood behind Jesus, weeping. Her tears fell upon His feet. She wiped them with her hair, kissed His feet, and anointed them.
Simon saw a sinner whose presence raised questions about Jesus.
Jesus saw a woman whose response revealed profound love in connection with forgiveness.
Simon questioned whether Jesus truly understood who was touching Him.
Jesus understood far more than Simon realized.
He knew her past.
He knew Simon's thoughts.
And He knew the difference between religious self-confidence and the gratitude of someone who understands the magnitude of forgiveness.
Jesus ultimately told her that her sins were forgiven and that her faith had saved her.
“Go in peace.”
What an extraordinary reversal.
The person who appeared least worthy in the room became the living illustration of forgiven love.
And the religious host became the recipient of a lesson about his own spiritual condition.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin does not matter.
But that the holy Son of God receives sinners who come to Him in faith, forgives them, and calls them into a new life.
Religion distorted by pride asks, “How could someone like you come near God?”
The Gospel declares that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
Paul understood this personally.
In 1 Timothy 1:13–16, he described his former life as a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent opponent of Christ's people. Yet he received mercy.
His past became a testimony to Christ's extraordinary patience.
The man who once persecuted believers became a servant of the Gospel.
Not because Paul successfully erased his history.
Because Jesus rewrote his future.
Perhaps that is why Matthew 23:13 should disturb every Christian who has ever forgotten what it cost to bring us into God's family.
None of us entered the kingdom because our religious résumé impressed God.
None of us purchased forgiveness with donations.
None of us earned eternal life through public recognition, ministry titles, church attendance, or moral superiority.
Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works, and that those saved in Christ are created for good works.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not its purchase price.
And yet how easily forgiven people forget that they were once in desperate need of forgiveness.
How easily rescued people become impatient with those who are still drowning.
How easily people who received mercy begin acting as though mercy belongs exclusively to them.
We can defend biblical truth without becoming cruel.
We can confront sin without humiliating sinners.
We can uphold holiness without pretending we have never needed grace.
We can practice discernment without surrendering to self-righteousness.
Galatians 6:1 instructs spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in a transgression with a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
Biblical correction is not supposed to be a performance of superiority.
Its purpose includes restoration.
There is a profound difference between warning someone about a cliff and pushing them toward it because they failed to listen.
There is a difference between calling someone to repentance and convincing them that repentance could never restore them.
There is a difference between faithfully preaching the narrow way and placing human-made obstacles across it.
Jesus Himself taught that the way leading to life is narrow (Matthew 7:13–14).
We must never confuse removing human barriers with removing Christ's commands.
We are not called to rewrite the Gospel to make sin comfortable.
We are called to proclaim the Gospel faithfully so sinners can discover that freedom, forgiveness, and reconciliation with God are found in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy of Matthew 23 is revealed near the end of the chapter.
After His severe warnings, Jesus lamented over Jerusalem.
“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem… how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” — Matthew 23:37
Do you see the heart behind the warning?
The same Jesus who pronounced judgment against hypocrisy also expressed the tenderness of gathering children beneath protective wings.
His holiness was not separated from His compassion.
His compassion did not cancel His holiness.
He confronted rebellion while revealing the tragedy of resisting God's invitation.
And eventually, that same Jesus went to the cross.
The One who exposed religious hypocrisy would suffer public humiliation.
The One who proclaimed forgiveness would bear the judgment sinners deserved.
The One who welcomed the repentant would be crucified between criminals.
There, according to Luke 23:39–43, a dying criminal turned toward Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build a religious reputation.
No years remaining to demonstrate his transformation.
No wealth with which to purchase mercy.
He acknowledged his guilt, recognized Jesus' innocence, and appealed to Christ's kingdom.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”
Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
A condemned man.
A crucified Savior.
A promise of paradise.
If anyone ever wondered whether a ruined past could place a repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ's mercy, look toward that cross.
The criminal did not save himself.
Jesus saved him.
And through His death and resurrection, Jesus accomplished what no religious institution, spiritual leader, human tradition, or financial contribution could ever accomplish.
He opened the way of reconciliation with God.
Hebrews 10:19–22 teaches that believers have confidence to enter God's presence through the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way He opened for us.
That is why Jesus could declare:
“I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved.” — John 10:9
The Greek word for door is θύρα (thyra).
Jesus did not merely claim to know where the door was.
He declared Himself to be the door.
He is not one religious option among many paths to reconciliation with the Father. In John 14:6, He identifies Himself as the way, the truth, and the life.
Our responsibility is not to replace Him.
It is to point people toward Him.
And now, this passage becomes deeply personal.
Maybe you have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Maybe you have been guilty of it.
Maybe you have been both the person standing outside the door and the person making it difficult for someone else to enter.
There is grace for the repentant.
But repentance requires honesty.
Ask Jesus to expose the pride you have disguised as discernment, the bitterness you have disguised as righteousness, and the cruelty you have excused as boldness.
Ask Him to heal the wounds that have made you afraid to trust again.

And remember that forgiveness does not require returning to an abusive environment or pretending that wrongdoing never happened. Biblical mercy does not eliminate the need for accountability, wisdom, justice, or appropriate boundaries.
You can seek healing without denying what happened.
You can pursue Christ without defending the people who misrepresented Him.
You can begin again.
Or perhaps your prayer today is simply, “Jesus, heal what religion wounded.”
You do not owe the internet your private struggles. But your testimony, when freely shared, may remind someone else that they are not alone.
You may never know who reads it.
You may never hear their testimony.
But you can help put biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Our mission is not to build another religious pedestal.
It is to point people toward the Savior.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers should give willingly, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Giving can glorify God when it flows from gratitude, love, generosity, and a sincere desire to serve Him.
Become part of a community committed to biblical truth, deeper discipleship, spiritual growth, and making Jesus Christ known.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
And it is not a measurement of your spiritual worth.
Whether you can contribute financially or not, your prayers, encouragement, and willingness to share the Gospel matter.
We must never become the very thing Jesus warned against in Matthew 23:13 by placing a financial barrier between people and the good news of salvation.
The Gospel must remain a proclamation of freely offered grace through Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the door.
One day, our titles will mean nothing.
Our followers, public recognition, religious achievements, and carefully constructed reputations will not be the foundation of our salvation.
Our only hope will be Jesus Christ.
So may we never become so occupied with appearing holy that we forget to love.
May we never become so confident in our knowledge that we refuse correction.
May we never become so protective of our religious reputation that we conceal injustice.
May we never use the name of Jesus to build walls that His Gospel calls people to cross through repentance and faith.
And if someone has convinced you that your past is too scandalous, your failures too numerous, or your wounds too deep for Christ to receive you, remember the woman who wept at His feet.
Remember the persecutor who received mercy.
Remember the criminal who turned toward Him on the cross.
Above all, remember the Savior who died and rose again.
Come to Him.
Not with excuses.
Not with a performance.
Not with a desperate attempt to purchase what only grace can provide.
Come in repentance and faith.
The hands of Jesus bear the wounds of the price He paid.
Never let the hands of someone who wounded you become the reason you refuse to reach for the nail-scarred hands of the One who came to save you.
